title: Write fields a strict receiver can split

blocks.text: The certification team tests a new receiver by feeding it raw ISO 8583 messages that a small tool writes by hand, without a packager. The receiver is strict: anything it can't read exactly as its specification says, it rejects, and a message the tool gets wrong costs a test slot. The tool's `FieldWriter` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/FieldWriter.java` writes one field at a time, from the format as the specification gives it (`n4`, `ans15`, `n..28`, `ans...300`) and the value.
It already parses the format. Finish the three methods marked `TODO`:

items: `allowed`: whether the receiver would accept the value's characters for that type;
`fixed`: a fixed field, as the receiver will take it;
`variable`: a variable field, as the receiver will take it.

blocks.text: When the receiver would reject a value, `write` must refuse it with an `IllegalArgumentException` rather than send something else. About 15 lines in total.

cases.says: fields that already fit their formats are written so that a receiver splits them back into the same values
a short numeric value is filled on the left with zeros, so the number the receiver reads is the one that was meant
a value longer than its field allows is refused, fixed or variable, never cut to fit
a variable field is its length and its own characters, never filled to its maximum
an LLLVAR field's length has three digits, whatever the value's length
a value with a character its type doesn't allow is refused, since the length alone proves nothing

origin.section: 3.2. A Short Value Is Padded, a Long One Is Refused, and Nothing Else Is Checked

concepts: Nothing in the bytes marks where a field ends: a fixed field takes its width and a variable one its length prefix, two digits for LLVAR and three for LLLVAR.
A short fixed value is padded (numbers with zeros on the left, text with spaces on the right) and a value that is too long is refused, never cut.
